extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, patent owners, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for compliance with the duty of candor, good faith, and disclosure (37 CFR 1.56 and 1.555) during patent prosecution, reexamination, supplemental examination, and related proceedings, including what information must be disclosed, who has the duty, materiality standards, and remedies for noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose information material to patentability (37 CFR 1.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each individual associated with the filing and prosecution of a patent application has a duty of candor and good faith in dealing with the Office, which includes a duty to disclose to the Office all information known to that individual to be material to patentability as defined in this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duty exists with respect to each pending claim until cancelled or withdrawn or application abandoned. No duty to submit information not material to any existing claim. Failure to disclose material information or fraud on the Office prevents grant of a patent. The Office encourages careful examination of foreign search reports and the closest information over which claims patentably define.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality standard under 37 CFR 1.56(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is material to patentability when it is not cumulative and (1) establishes, by itself or in combination with other information, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) refutes, or is inconsistent with, a position the applicant takes in opposing an Office rejection or asserting patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prima facie case of unpatentability is established when the information compels a conclusion that a claim is unpatentable under the preponderance of the evidence standard, giving each claim term its broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, and before considering applicant's evidence to the contrary. In close cases, applicants should consider submitting the information; the Office may consider harmonizing materiality to a 'but-for' standard consistent with Therasense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who has the duty to disclose (37 CFR 1.56(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals having the duty include (1) each inventor named in the application; (2) each attorney or agent who prepares or prosecutes the application; and (3) every other person who is substantively involved in the preparation or prosecution of the application and who is associated with the inventor, applicant, assignee, or anyone to whom there is an obligation to assign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duty applies to individuals, not organizations; typists, clerks, and similar personnel not substantively involved are not covered. For reexamination, analogous duties apply to the patent owner and those substantively involved on behalf of the patent owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: To whom the duty is owed: the Office (USPTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of candor and good faith is owed in dealing with the Office and includes a duty to disclose to the Office material information. The duty extends beyond examiner interactions to proceedings before the PTAB and Commissioner for Patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All dealings with the USPTO count; statements to other USPTO officials or in PTAB proceedings are within the scope of the duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of reasonable inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party presenting a paper to the USPTO has a duty to perform an inquiry that is reasonable under the circumstances to determine whether material information exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable inquiry may include reviewing documents submitted to or received from other government agencies, reviewing communications, and investigating potential material facts. Failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry can be evidence of lack of candor and may support inequitable conduct findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to correct erroneous or inconsistent statements promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party discovers that an earlier position made to the USPTO or another government agency was incorrect or inconsistent with other statements, the party must promptly correct the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correction may be required even if the original incorrect statement was made without deceptive intent (post-AIA changes). Failure to correct may result in practitioner discipline or inequitable conduct consequences (see In re Tendler example).

rubrics_metrics.name: When the duty applies in time (continuing duty until grant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty to disclose information exists until the application becomes abandoned and extends until a patent is granted on that application; applicants may submit information after allowance but before payment of the issue fee under specified rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IDS filings under 37 CFR 1.97/1.98 permit submission after allowance in some circumstances; withdrawing an application from issue is possible under certain provisions to allow consideration of new information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction of duty by proper citation or submission (IDS rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty to disclose all information known to be material to patentability is deemed satisfied if such information was cited by the Office or submitted to the Office in the manner prescribed by §§ 1.97(b)-(d) and 1.98.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an Information Disclosure Statement per the rules provides certainty when information will be considered, and the Office will inform applicants when information is not considered. Even if previously cited, a document may trigger reexamination if it raises a substantial new question of patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners' authority to require information under 37 CFR 1.105
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examiners may require submission of information reasonably necessary to properly examine or treat a matter in a pending or abandoned application, even if that information is not material to patentability under 37 CFR 1.56.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such requirements can include documents submitted to other government agencies (e.g., FDA filings) when reasonably necessary to examine a claim (e.g., manufacturing process details). See MPEP § 704.12(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'information' that may be material
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Information' includes prior art (patents, publications) and other information such as enablement issues, possible prior public uses, sales, offers to sell, derived knowledge, prior invention by another, litigation statements, inventorship conflicts, regulatory submissions, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materiality not limited to classic prior art; any information a reasonable examiner would be substantially likely to consider important in deciding patentability is material. However, information favorable to patentability (e.g., commercial success) or material solely to level of ordinary skill is not required by the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of information do not affect duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Materiality controls whether information must be disclosed, not the circumstances under which or the source from which the information is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information learned from co-workers, trade shows, communications with competitors, related foreign applications, copending US applications, litigation, regulatory submissions, or third parties must be disclosed if material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art cited in related foreign applications is presumptively material
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants and associated individuals have a duty to bring to the Office any material prior art or other information cited or brought to their attention in any related foreign application; such references are especially likely material if used to reject similar claims abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign counsel and applicants must ensure adverse foreign-cited references are communicated to US prosecution counsel and to the USPTO; withholding such foreign-cited prior art can lead to inequitable conduct findings (Gemveto example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of copending United States patent applications and their prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals must bring to the examiner's attention other copending US applications that are material to patentability of the application under examination, including identification of pending or abandoned applications by the same inventors or assignee that disclose similar subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the examiner is aware of related applications; disclose similar applications and the prior art cited therein when material. When an application is a continuation/divisional/CIP, the examiner will consider prior art properly cited in earlier applications as noted in related MPEP sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of information from litigation or trial proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: When subject matter is involved in litigation or PTAB trial proceedings or such proceedings yield information material to pending related patent applications, the existence of such litigation and material information arising therefrom must be brought to the attention of the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material litigation information includes prior public use/sales evidence, inventorship questions, prior art, allegations of fraud or inequitable conduct, and any assertions contradictory to positions made to the examiner. Copies of court papers should accompany reissue applications when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification when claims are copied from a patent (37 CFR 41.202(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claims are copied or substantially copied from a patent, the applicant must identify the source patent and the numbers of the patent claims at the time the copied claims are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information about copying is material under 37 CFR 1.56; failure to identify copied claims may violate the duty of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory submissions (e.g., FDA) may be material and must be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentation submitted to regulatory review bodies that is material to any pending patent application or reexamination proceeding should be submitted to the USPTO for review; contradictory assertions in regulatory submissions may be material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include FDA NDAs/BLA materials and Paragraph IV certifications. Listing on FDA compilations does not satisfy USPTO disclosure requirements; applicants should consider providing factual and legal bases when intended to list a patent in the Orange Book. See Belcher Pharmaceuticals and MPEP § 2164.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality exclusions: not required to disclose information favorable to patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure rules are not intended to require submission of information favorable to patentability, such as evidence of commercial success, or information concerning level of skill in the art for obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants need not disclose every piece of evidence; focus on information a reasonable examiner would consider important to patentability issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, disclose (close cases guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In close cases where materiality or consistency is uncertain, the applicant should consider submitting the information to the USPTO to strengthen the patent and avoid later risks on materiality or intent determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO expects many applicants will choose to submit marginal information to avoid incorrect judgments on materiality; the Office holds individuals to high standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of fraud, inequitable conduct, or violation of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of fraud, inequitable conduct, or violation of the duty of disclosure with respect to any claim in an application or patent renders all the claims thereof unenforceable or invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat inequitable conduct as affecting the patent as a whole — an all-or-nothing consequence. Cases (e.g., Therasense) inform the materiality and intent analysis; the USPTO has proposed rule changes to harmonize materiality with the 'but-for' standard. Evidence of intent to deceive or bad faith is central to inequitable conduct findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of disclosure in reexamination and supplemental examination (37 CFR 1.555 et seq.)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reexamination proceedings the patent owner, its attorneys/agents, and others substantively involved on behalf of the owner have a duty of candor and to disclose all information known to be material to patentability in the proceeding; similar duties apply in supplemental examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IDS should be filed with items listed in § 1.98(a) and generally within two months of the reexamination order. Failure to comply may be noted as unresolved questions under § 1.552(c) and may be referred to the U.S. Attorney General if supplemental examination reveals possible material fraud on the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties arising from dealings with other government agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals with a duty to disclose should ensure statements made to the USPTO and other government agencies (e.g., FDA) are consistent; providing material information to other agencies while withholding it from the USPTO undermines the duty of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include inconsistent statements between FDA submissions and USPTO prosecution positions (Belcher Pharms.). Parties receiving Paragraph IV certifications or other ANDA-related documents should review for materiality to pending USPTO matters and submit material information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on deliberate schemes to prevent knowledge (walling off)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate schemes or established practices to prevent individuals with a duty to disclose from obtaining knowledge of material information (e.g., walling off prosecution practitioners from others) are inconsistent with candor and good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have refused to enforce patents where patentee suppressed material information (Keystone Driller, Precision Instruments). Practices that intentionally withhold material information from prosecution counsel may support inequitable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty applies to individuals associated with patent owner (not the organization itself)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of disclosure applies to individuals, and actions of such individuals may affect the rights of their employing corporation or institution; the duty does not attach to an organization as a legal entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals within a corporation who are substantively involved in preparation or prosecution bear the duty; organizational separation does not absolve individual duty.
